tokens.name: Accessibility Mode
tokens.definition: The primary accessibility design orientation of the learning experience.

values.definition: Standard accessibility compliance (WCAG 2.1 AA).
Designed to function in limited connectivity environments.
Content is primarily designed for screen reader accessibility.
Content is available in multiple sensory modalities.
Time-based constraints are minimized or eliminated.
Full Universal Design for Learning principles applied.

tokens.name: Accessibility Media Alternatives
tokens.definition: The accessible alternatives provided for media-based content.

values.definition: Synchronized text captions for video or audio content.
Full text transcript of audio or video content.
Text descriptions of images and visual content.
Print-ready versions of all materials.
Audio narration of visual information for video content.
All assets available for offline download.

tokens.name: Agency Mode
tokens.definition: The degree of learner choice and self-direction in the learning experience.

values.definition: The learner follows a predetermined sequence with no choices.
The learner chooses within defined options provided by the instructor.
The learner defines their own direction within the domain.
The learner sets goals, selects methods, and evaluates their own progress.

tokens.name: Agency Choice Point
tokens.definition: The dimension(s) where learner choice is exercised.

values.definition: Learner chooses what to study or investigate.
Learner chooses which tools or technologies to use.
Learner chooses the output format or medium.
Learner chooses the order of activities.
Learner chooses collaborators.
Learner chooses the form of the final product.
Learner chooses who their work is for.

tokens.name: AI Use Policy
tokens.definition: The policy governing learner use of AI tools in this activity.
tokens.aiGuidance: Never set to anything other than prohibited without also setting aiUse.disclosureRequired to true.

values.definition: AI tools are not permitted in this activity.
No AI use policy has been defined. Not recommended for new content.
The instructor will specify AI use rules outside this content block.
AI use is permitted but disclosure is not required. Use sparingly.
AI assistance is permitted and must be disclosed.
AI is used as a collaborative partner; disclosure and reflection required.
Learners are explicitly using AI as the subject of investigation.

tokens.name: AI Allowed Functions
tokens.definition: The specific AI functions permitted in this activity.
tokens.aiGuidance: Be specific. List only permitted functions. Never leave unspecified when aiUse.policy is not prohibited.

values.definition: AI may be used to brainstorm and generate initial ideas.
AI may be used to create outlines and structural plans.
AI may be used to debug code or identify logical errors.
AI may be used to critique drafts or designs.
AI may be used to provide feedback on drafts or work-in-progress.
AI may be used to generate or locate references and sources.
AI may be used to generate images.
AI may be used to generate code.
AI may be used to generate the final submission artifact.

tokens.name: AI Disclosure Required
tokens.definition: Whether learners must disclose their AI use in this activity.

tokens.name: AI Reflection Required
tokens.definition: Whether learners must submit a reflection on their AI use.

tokens.name: Assessment Evidence
tokens.definition: The primary form of evidence collected to demonstrate learning.

values.definition: A knowledge check or test with predetermined correct answers.
A tangible product created by the learner.
A live or recorded demonstration of skill.
A curated collection of work over time.
Written or recorded personal reflection on learning.
Documentation produced during a critique or review session.
Evidence of the learning process itself (sketches, drafts, logs).
A structured presentation to an audience.
A finished product accompanied by a required reflection.

tokens.name: Assessment Mode
tokens.definition: The purpose or function of the assessment in the learning arc.

values.definition: Assessment used to guide ongoing learning; low-stakes.
Assessment of learning at the end of a unit; higher-stakes.
Assessment used to identify prior knowledge or gaps before instruction.
Assessment comparing learner to their own prior performance.
Assessment that must be passed at a threshold before advancement.
Assessment conducted through structured group critique.

tokens.name: Collaboration Structure
tokens.definition: How learners are organized for collaborative work.

values.definition: Each learner works alone.
Learners work in pairs.
Learners work in groups of 3-6.
Learners review each other's work in a structured exchange.
Work is shared and critiqued in a group critique format.
Collaboration involves a real external community partner.

tokens.name: Collaboration Role Clarity
tokens.definition: How explicitly roles are defined within collaborative work.

values.definition: No role definitions given.
Roles emerge organically without formal assignment.
Specific roles are assigned by the instructor.
Roles rotate across activities or sessions.

tokens.name: Feedback Mode
tokens.definition: Who provides feedback on learner work.

values.definition: No feedback is given.
Learner evaluates their own work.
Another learner provides feedback.
The instructor provides feedback.
Feedback is system-generated.
Feedback comes from a community partner or external audience.
Both peer and instructor feedback are provided.
Multiple feedback sources are used.

tokens.name: Feedback Timing
tokens.definition: When feedback is provided relative to the submission or activity.

values.definition: Feedback is given before the learner finalizes work (e.g., draft review).
Feedback is given during the activity (e.g., coaching, in-process check-ins).
Feedback is given after the learner submits.
Multiple rounds of feedback are built into the design.
Learner requests feedback when ready.

tokens.name: Localization Level
tokens.definition: The depth of localization applied to the learning materials.

values.definition: No localization. Original language and examples only.
Text is translated but examples remain from the original cultural context.
Both language and examples are adapted to the target cultural context.
Deeper cultural adaptation including values, norms, and local context.
Materials were co-designed with members of the target community.

tokens.name: Bandwidth Assumption
tokens.definition: The assumed internet connectivity level for learners.

values.definition: Assumes limited or intermittent connectivity (< 1 Mbps).
Assumes moderate broadband connectivity.
Assumes reliable high-speed internet.
All materials must function without internet access.

tokens.name: Reflection Required
tokens.definition: Whether structured reflection is a required component of the learning activity.

tokens.name: Reflection Focus
tokens.definition: The subject or lens of the required reflection.

values.definition: Reflecting on how the learner approached the task.
Reflecting on how concepts apply to other contexts.
Reflecting on aesthetic or design decisions made.
Reflecting on ethical dimensions, especially AI use or community impact.
Reflecting on how the group worked together.
Reflecting on what didn't work and why.
Reflecting on one's own learning and thinking strategies.

tokens.name: Revision Required
tokens.definition: Whether learners are required to revise their work after feedback.

tokens.name: Revision Mode
tokens.definition: The structure of the revision requirement.

values.definition: Revision is available but not required.
One revision cycle is required.
The learner must revise until meeting the proficiency threshold.
Multiple structured revision cycles are built into the design.

tokens.name: Scaffolding Level
tokens.definition: The degree of instructional support provided to the learner.
tokens.aiGuidance: Match scaffolding level to learner experience. Beginners need high; advanced learners benefit from low to build agency.

values.definition: No scaffolding. Learner must self-direct entirely.
Minimal prompts or guiding questions only.
values.useWhen: Intermediate to advanced learners with prior domain knowledge.

values.definition: Some structure, examples, or guiding questions provided.
values.useWhen: Mixed experience levels; most adult learners.

values.definition: Worked examples, templates, checklists, and step-by-step guidance.
values.useWhen: Novice or early-stage learners; high-stakes tasks.

values.definition: Scaffolding adjusts dynamically based on learner progress.

tokens.name: Scaffolding Type
tokens.definition: The primary modality of instructional support provided.
tokens.aiGuidance: Use in combination with scaffolding.level. If scaffolding.level is high, specify the scaffolding.type so AI agents can generate the right support materials.

values.definition: A solved problem or completed example provided for reference.
A list of steps or criteria the learner can check off.
A partially completed structure for the learner to fill in.
A sequential set of instructions that walk the learner through the task.
A high-quality example of a finished product for comparison.
Ongoing feedback from an instructor or peer throughout the process.
No scaffolding type. Used with scaffolding.level none.

patterns.name: Artifact Analysis Reflection
patterns.summary: Learners closely analyze an existing artifact, then reflect on its significance, method, and meaning.
patterns.problem: How do you develop close reading and critical analysis skills through artifact engagement?
context: Retrospective learning (analyzing your own past work)
Any course emphasizing interpretive or analytical skills

sequence.label: Artifact Encounter
sequence.learnerAction: Encounter the artifact without interpretive guidance. Note your initial reactions, observations, and questions.
sequence.instructorAction: Select artifact and withhold context. Ask for unguided first impressions before providing background.

sequence.label: Contextual Analysis
sequence.learnerAction: Learn the context of the artifact's creation (historical, cultural, authorial). Re-examine the artifact through that context. Note how your reading shifts.
sequence.instructorAction: Provide relevant contextual information. Facilitate discussion of how context changes interpretation.

sequence.label: Close Reading
sequence.learnerAction: Conduct a structured close reading using an analysis framework (semiotics, rhetorical analysis, formal analysis, etc.). Document specific evidence from the artifact.
sequence.instructorAction: Provide the analysis framework. Require evidence citation from the artifact itself.

sequence.label: Significance Reflection
sequence.learnerAction: Write a reflection on what this artifact means, why it matters, and what you understand differently having studied it.
sequence.instructorAction: Assess both the analytical rigor of the close reading and the depth of the significance reflection.

patterns.aiGuidance: When generating close reading prompts, specify the analysis framework explicitly. Do not ask for "what do you think?" — ask for evidence-anchored claims. The significance reflection should push beyond description to interpretation and personal meaning-making.

patterns.name: Case, Stakeholder Analysis, Response Design
patterns.summary: Learners examine a complex case, analyze the perspectives of affected stakeholders, and design a justified response.
patterns.problem: How do you develop ethical reasoning and policy thinking in courses where there are no simple right answers?

sequence.label: Case Presentation
sequence.learnerAction: Read, watch, or listen to a case study representing a complex real-world problem. Take notes on the key facts, actors, and tensions.
sequence.instructorAction: Present or curate the case. Provide sufficient context for learners to understand complexity. Do not resolve tensions prematurely.

sequence.label: Stakeholder Identification
sequence.learnerAction: Identify all stakeholders affected by the situation. Document each stakeholder's interests, constraints, and likely perspective.
sequence.instructorAction: Provide a stakeholder analysis scaffold. Ensure learners include marginalized and non-obvious stakeholders.

sequence.label: Perspective Analysis
sequence.learnerAction: Write or present a brief perspective statement from each key stakeholder's point of view. Identify tensions between stakeholder interests.
sequence.instructorAction: Facilitate perspective-taking discussion. Challenge oversimplifications.

sequence.label: Response Design
sequence.learnerAction: Design and justify a response to the case that acknowledges stakeholder interests and states trade-offs explicitly.
sequence.instructorAction: Assess response on clarity of reasoning, acknowledgment of complexity, and quality of justification — not on position taken.

patterns.aiGuidance: When generating content for this pattern, do not resolve the case tensions. Provide a rich, ambiguous case. Scaffold the stakeholder analysis before the response design phase. The assessment should not privilege any single political or ethical stance.

patterns.name: Community-Contextualized Design Brief
patterns.summary: Learners design a real artifact for a real community partner, contextualizing all production decisions in community needs.
patterns.problem: How do you create authentic learning experiences that generate real value for real people outside the classroom?
context: Courses with explicit equity and social justice goals

sequence.label: Community Partner Introduction
sequence.learnerAction: Meet or learn about the community partner. Document the partner's context, needs, constraints, and goals. Resist proposing solutions at this stage.
sequence.instructorAction: Arrange community partner engagement. Scaffold active listening. Suppress the "design instinct" to jump to solutions.

sequence.label: Needs Analysis
sequence.learnerAction: Analyze the partner's needs through the lens of this course's skills and knowledge. Identify what you can realistically offer and what is beyond scope.
sequence.instructorAction: Guide learners to calibrate ambition to capacity. Ensure learners are not over-promising.

sequence.label: Design and Iteration
sequence.learnerAction: Design an artifact addressing a specific documented need. Share drafts or prototypes with the partner for feedback. Revise in response to partner input.
sequence.instructorAction: Facilitate partner feedback sessions. Ensure learners are listening, not defending.
sequence.evidence: draft artifact plus partner feedback documentation

sequence.label: Delivery and Reflection
sequence.learnerAction: Deliver the final artifact to the partner. Reflect on the design process, the community context, your role, and what you would do differently.
sequence.instructorAction: Assess both artifact quality and quality of reflection on community engagement.

patterns.aiGuidance: When generating design briefs for this pattern, center the community partner's actual stated needs. Do not invent a community or fabricate needs. If generating a simulated partner, make the simulation explicit. Reflection should engage with power dynamics and positionality, not just process description.

patterns.name: Constraint-Based Project Sprint
patterns.summary: Learners produce an artifact under explicit constraints, emphasizing rapid iteration and decisive creative choices.
patterns.problem: How do you develop creative confidence and decision-making speed in learners who over-plan and under-produce?
context: Any course emphasizing production throughput over perfection

sequence.label: Brief and Constraints
sequence.learnerAction: Receive the project brief and explicit constraints (time limit, material restrictions, required elements, excluded approaches). Ask clarifying questions.
sequence.instructorAction: State constraints clearly and explain their purpose. Constraints should be meaningful, not arbitrary.

sequence.label: Rapid Ideation
sequence.learnerAction: Generate multiple divergent ideas (3–5 minimum) before committing to any. Use sketches, outlines, or quick prototypes.
sequence.instructorAction: Facilitate timed ideation. Encourage quantity over quality at this phase.

sequence.label: Committed Production
sequence.learnerAction: Select one direction and produce a complete artifact within the allotted time. Prioritize completion over perfection.
sequence.instructorAction: Set and hold firm time limits. Resist requests for extensions — deadline pressure is pedagogically intentional.

sequence.label: Process Debrief
sequence.learnerAction: Reflect on the constraints: which helped, which hurt, what decisions you would change, and what the constraint revealed about your process.
sequence.instructorAction: Facilitate whole-class debrief. Focus on creative decision-making under pressure.

patterns.aiGuidance: Generate constraints that are specific and meaningful. Avoid constraints that merely restrict scope without shaping creative decisions. The debrief prompt should ask about constraint experience, not just artifact quality.

patterns.name: Demo, Guided Practice, Independent Production
patterns.summary: Instructor demonstrates a skill or technique, learners practice with support, then apply independently.
patterns.problem: How do you teach procedural or technical skills to novices who need to see before they do?

sequence.label: Demonstration
sequence.learnerAction: Observe the instructor demonstration. Take notes on each step and note points of difficulty or confusion.
sequence.instructorAction: Demonstrate the target skill step-by-step while narrating decisions and common mistakes. Use think-aloud protocol.

sequence.label: Guided Practice
sequence.learnerAction: Attempt the skill with a provided scaffold (template, checklist, guided worksheet, or worked example). Ask questions as needed.
sequence.instructorAction: Circulate or monitor asynchronous submissions. Provide targeted feedback. Allow multiple attempts on the guided exercise.

sequence.label: Formative Check
sequence.learnerAction: Receive instructor or peer feedback on guided practice. Identify gaps and revise before independent work.
sequence.instructorAction: Provide written or verbal feedback. Identify patterns across class and address common errors.

sequence.label: Independent Production
sequence.learnerAction: Apply the skill without scaffolding to a new but analogous task. Produce the final artifact.
sequence.instructorAction: Assess independently produced work against criteria. Offer revision opportunity if appropriate.

patterns.aiGuidance: When generating content for this pattern, produce a demonstration walkthrough first, then a scaffolded exercise version, then an independent exercise version. Each version should clearly state its scaffolding level.

patterns.name: Mastery Checkpoint Pathway
patterns.summary: Learners progress through skill levels, demonstrating mastery at each checkpoint before advancing.
patterns.problem: How do you ensure all learners reach genuine proficiency before moving to the next skill level?
context: Any course where prerequisite mastery matters

sequence.label: Skill Introduction
sequence.learnerAction: Review the learning objective and mastery criteria for this checkpoint. Understand what proficiency looks like before beginning.
sequence.instructorAction: Present the skill in context. Make the mastery criteria explicit. Connect to prior skills.

sequence.label: Scaffolded Practice
sequence.learnerAction: Work through scaffolded practice exercises from guided to independent. Identify where errors occur and use them as learning signals.
sequence.instructorAction: Provide worked examples, then remove scaffolding gradually. Allow unlimited low-stakes attempts.

sequence.label: Checkpoint Attempt
sequence.learnerAction: Attempt the mastery checkpoint. This is a genuine demonstration, not a practice exercise.
sequence.instructorAction: Evaluate against explicit mastery criteria. Pass or not-yet. If not-yet, provide specific feedback on gaps.

sequence.label: Remediation and Re-attempt (if needed)
sequence.learnerAction: If not-yet, address specific gaps identified in feedback. Attempt additional practice. Re-attempt the checkpoint.
sequence.instructorAction: Facilitate targeted remediation. Ensure the re-attempt tests the same objective with a parallel (not identical) task.

patterns.aiGuidance: When generating checkpoint assessments, ensure the mastery criteria are specific and observable. Scaffolded practice and checkpoint should test the same skill with different tasks. Mastery is binary (pass/not-yet) — not a gradient.

patterns.name: Observe, Analyze, Create, Critique, Revise
patterns.summary: A studio-based cycle where learners study exemplars, analyze structure, make original work, receive critique, and revise.
patterns.problem: How do you design a learning experience where making, feedback, and revision are the core of learning — not supplemental?

sequence.label: Observe
sequence.learnerAction: Study 2-3 exemplars of finished work in the target form.
sequence.instructorAction: Curate exemplars that represent the range of quality and approach. Prompt observation with guiding questions.

sequence.label: Analyze
sequence.learnerAction: Identify patterns, techniques, decisions, and what makes each exemplar effective or not.
sequence.instructorAction: Facilitate structured analysis using a common vocabulary or rubric.

sequence.label: Create
sequence.learnerAction: Produce original work in response to the brief.
sequence.instructorAction: Circulate, offer coaching feedback during process.

sequence.label: Critique
sequence.learnerAction: Present work to peers; receive structured feedback using established criteria.
sequence.instructorAction: Facilitate critique. Model feedback language. Keep critique focused on work, not person.

sequence.label: Revise
sequence.learnerAction: Revise work based on critique. Document what changed and why.
sequence.instructorAction: Review revision with attention to responsiveness to feedback.

patterns.aiGuidance: When generating materials for this pattern, produce both a student-facing brief (phases 1-5 as instructions) and a studio critique guide for the instructor. Ensure the exemplars section specifies what to observe. Do not skip the revision phase.

patterns.name: Peer Review Studio Cycle
patterns.summary: Learners produce a draft, give and receive structured peer critique, then revise based on feedback.
patterns.problem: How do you build a culture of critical feedback and iterative improvement in a writing or production course?
context: Any course with iterative production and revision

sequence.label: Draft Production
sequence.learnerAction: Produce a complete first draft or prototype. Label it clearly as a draft and identify two or three areas you want feedback on.
sequence.instructorAction: Set clear draft submission requirements. Clarify what "complete draft" means — not a rough outline.

sequence.label: Peer Critique
sequence.learnerAction: Review an assigned peer's draft using a structured critique guide. Provide specific, evidence-based feedback. Avoid vague praise or criticism.
sequence.instructorAction: Provide a critique guide with explicit criteria. Facilitate brief norms discussion before critique begins.

sequence.label: Feedback Reception
sequence.learnerAction: Read all peer feedback. Identify patterns. Ask clarifying questions if needed. Do not defend your draft at this stage.
sequence.instructorAction: Facilitate structured feedback reception (optional). Ensure learners are reading, not dismissing, peer feedback.

sequence.label: Revision
sequence.learnerAction: Revise the artifact in response to feedback. Document which feedback you acted on and why, and which you chose not to use and why.
sequence.instructorAction: Review revision documentation alongside final artifact. Assess the quality of revision reasoning, not just the artifact.

patterns.aiGuidance: When generating critique guides, provide specific criteria anchored to the learning objectives — not generic writing advice. The revision memo is as important as the artifact. Assess reasoning, not just outcomes.

patterns.name: Prompt, AI Experiment, Evaluate, Disclose
patterns.summary: Learners craft a prompt, run an AI experiment, critically evaluate the output, and disclose their process.
patterns.problem: How do you teach critical AI use when learners lack frameworks for evaluating AI output?
context: Any course that permits or requires AI tool use

sequence.label: Prompt Design
sequence.learnerAction: Design and document a prompt intended to produce a specified outcome. Consider specificity, context, and constraints.
sequence.instructorAction: Provide exemplar prompts and non-examples. Facilitate discussion of what makes a prompt effective.

sequence.label: AI Experiment
sequence.learnerAction: Run the prompt through one or more AI tools. Document the outputs without editing them.
sequence.instructorAction: Ensure access to appropriate tools. Clarify ethical and policy constraints on tool use.

sequence.label: Evaluate Output
sequence.learnerAction: Evaluate the AI output against explicit criteria: accuracy, bias, gaps, usefulness, limitations. Revise the prompt if needed and document iterations.
sequence.instructorAction: Provide an evaluation rubric. Facilitate whole-class discussion of common AI failure modes.

sequence.label: Disclose and Reflect
sequence.learnerAction: Complete an AI Use Disclosure (AIUL) documenting which tools were used, what functions they served, and what the learner contributed.
sequence.instructorAction: Review disclosures for completeness and accuracy.

patterns.aiGuidance: When scaffolding this pattern, provide explicit prompt design criteria and evaluation rubrics. Do not allow learners to submit AI output without evaluation. The AIUL declaration is required, not optional.

patterns.name: Reference Study, Technical Exercise, Creative Application
patterns.summary: Learners study exemplars, complete a technical exercise to build foundational skill, then apply it creatively.
patterns.problem: How do you help learners move from technical proficiency to creative ownership?
context: Any field combining technical skill and creative judgment

sequence.label: Reference Study
sequence.learnerAction: Study a curated set of exemplary works from practitioners in the field. Document specific techniques, decisions, and effects observed.
sequence.instructorAction: Curate exemplars representing diverse approaches and contexts. Provide an observation guide.

sequence.label: Technical Exercise
sequence.learnerAction: Complete a constrained technical exercise that isolates a specific technique observed in the reference study. Focus on precision and control.
sequence.instructorAction: Provide step-by-step guidance. Allow multiple attempts. Give targeted technical feedback.

sequence.label: Technique Reflection
sequence.learnerAction: Reflect on what the technique does and why practitioners might choose to use or avoid it.
sequence.instructorAction: Facilitate brief discussion connecting technique to context and intention.

sequence.label: Creative Application
sequence.learnerAction: Apply the studied technique(s) in an original work of your own design. Make intentional choices and document them.
sequence.instructorAction: Assess both the quality of technique and the intentionality of creative decisions.

patterns.aiGuidance: When generating exemplars for this pattern, include diverse practitioners and contexts. The creative application phase should specify that learners state their intention — not just submit a product.

themes.name: Accessibility-First
themes.summary: A Universal Design for Learning (UDL) style where accessibility is the primary design constraint, not an afterthought.
themes.aiGuidance: When applying this theme, every media asset must have an accessible alternative. Assessment evidence must not privilege any single modality. Provide multiple means of representation, expression, and engagement as defined by UDL. Assume all learners may have assistive technology needs.

themes.name: AI Literacy
themes.summary: A critical AI use style where AI tools are the subject of investigation — how they work, what they produce, and what they mean.
themes.aiGuidance: When applying this theme, AI tools are required, not optional. Learners must document their AI use, evaluate its outputs, and reflect on its implications. Assessment criteria must reward critical evaluation over AI output quality. The AI Use Disclosure (AIUL) is a required deliverable.

themes.name: Community-Engaged
themes.summary: A participatory learning style where real community partners shape the learning brief and receive real deliverables.
themes.aiGuidance: When applying this theme, the community partner's needs must frame the design brief. Learner reflection must address positionality, power, and what the learner's role is relative to the community. Simulated community partners are acceptable but must be explicitly labeled as simulations. Assessment should weigh community benefit and reflective depth, not just artifact quality.

themes.name: Constructivist Studio
themes.summary: A making-centred pedagogical style where learning happens through creating, critiquing, and revising work.
themes.description: The constructivist studio treats the act of making as the primary site of learning. Learners build understanding through production, not reception. Critique is collaborative and ongoing. Revision is expected and valued.
themes.aiGuidance: When generating materials for this theme, foreground making. The project brief should lead with the deliverable and the critique structure, not a reading list. Include a studio critique guide. Reflection should focus on process and creative choices.

themes.name: Critical Media Analysis
themes.summary: A representation-focused style where learners analyze how media constructs meaning, power, and identity, and respond creatively.
themes.aiGuidance: When applying this theme, analytical frameworks must be named explicitly (semiotics, representation theory, framing analysis, etc.). Creative response assignments should require learners to make and state intentional choices that engage with the critical analysis. Assessment criteria must reward analytical rigor, not ideological agreement.

themes.name: Direct Instruction
themes.summary: An explicit, instructor-led teaching style with demonstration, guided practice, and skill verification.
themes.aiGuidance: When applying this theme, lead with explicit learning objectives and connect each activity directly to an objective. Worked examples should precede practice. Assessments should test the same skill demonstrated. Keep agency minimal — the learner's job at this stage is to master the defined skill.

themes.name: Inquiry-Based
themes.summary: A question-driven investigative style where learners generate and pursue their own inquiries with instructor support.
themes.aiGuidance: When applying this theme, open with a question rather than a statement. Assessment criteria should reward quality of inquiry process as much as quality of conclusions. Resist giving answers too early — sustained productive discomfort is pedagogically valuable here.

themes.name: Low-Bandwidth Global
themes.summary: An OER delivery style designed for under-resourced and offline contexts, prioritizing downloadable assets and low-tech alternatives.
themes.aiGuidance: When applying this theme, every content element must have a low-bandwidth or offline equivalent. No auto-playing media. All assets must be downloadable. Avoid external service dependencies that require internet access at time of use. Assessment must be completable offline or via asynchronous submission.

themes.name: Mastery Learning
themes.summary: A competency-based style where learners demonstrate proficiency before advancing, with unlimited revision until mastery.
themes.aiGuidance: When applying this theme, make mastery criteria explicit and observable before the activity begins. Assessment is pass/not-yet — never graded on a curve. Re-attempts test the same objective with a parallel (not identical) task. Progress should be gated by demonstrated competency, not time spent.

themes.name: Project-Based Production
themes.summary: An extended authentic project style where learners produce a real artifact for a real or simulated audience through iterative development.
themes.aiGuidance: When applying this theme, ensure the project brief specifies a real or simulated audience with real constraints. Multiple feedback cycles before final submission are required, not optional. Assessment should weigh process documentation alongside final product quality.

validationRules.name: Learning Objective Requires Assessment Evidence
validationRules.message: No assessment evidence type is specified. Every learning activity must define how learning will be evidenced.
validationRules.rationale: Without a defined evidence type, there is no basis for evaluating whether learning occurred.

validationRules.name: Revision Requires Pre-Submission Feedback
validationRules.message: revision.required is true but feedback.timing is after-submission. Revision cannot be meaningfully performed without timely feedback.
validationRules.rationale: If feedback arrives only after submission, learners cannot revise in the same cycle.

validationRules.name: AI Use Requires Disclosure
validationRules.message: aiUse.policy permits AI use but aiUse.disclosureRequired is not set to true.
validationRules.rationale: Any non-prohibited AI use must require disclosure for academic integrity.

validationRules.name: Collaborative AI Use Requires Reflection
validationRules.message: aiUse.policy is collaborative-disclosed but reflection.required is not true. Collaborative AI use requires reflection.
validationRules.rationale: Collaborative AI use involves the highest degree of AI integration. Without reflection, learners cannot develop critical AI literacy.

validationRules.name: Low Bandwidth Requires Downloadable Alternatives
validationRules.message: bandwidth.assumption is low or offline-capable but no downloadable-assets media alternative is specified.
validationRules.rationale: Low-bandwidth learners need downloadable assets to access content offline.
